(Today through Saturday)...
Issued at 127 AM EDT Sun Jul 26 2026

Today:

Central Indiana will be within a transition zone early this morning 
into the afternoon as an upper level trough exits eastward and a 
broad ridge builds in from the west. Initially, this will promote 
subsidence through the mid-levels, and in combination with prior day 
low level saturation will maintain a compressed saturated layer near 
the surface throughout the morning hours. This saturated layer 
will likely remain thin enough to avoid drizzle formation, but 
there may be enough latent heat fluxes over the Wabash valley for 
pockets of dense fog between 09-12Z this morning.

As stated, central Indiana will remain within this transition zone 
until the ridge axis nears overnight. This transition will consist 
of moderate WAA over the area throughout the day. WAA along with 
weak westerly surface winds should mix out the low level saturated 
layer during the morning hours, with the remainder of the day 
consisting of mostly upper level clouds within the strong jet stream 
and blow off from upstream convection. The resulting temperatures 
are likely to push into the upper 80s this afternoon, but likely 
will stay below 90 as the cloud cover dampens the typical diurnal 
temperature curve. 

Forecast confidence is moderately high during the daytime today 
with one caveat, a current ongoing convective cluster over NW 
Iowa. The aforementioned transition zone will be narrow with a 
deep unstable airmass only a few hundred miles to the west of 
central Indiana. Although this area of convection is expected to 
pulsate throughout the night as it pushes to the E/SE, its 
resulting cold pool should remain consistent and will likely 
continue to initiate additional convective clusters over northern 
and central IL this morning. 

The CAPE gradient is expected to remain west of the Indiana border 
as this cold pool nears from the west, likely shifting the overall 
storm motion southward and keeping thunderstorms to the west of our 
area. That said, there is a low chance that the cold pool and 
resulting convection remains strong enough to push into the less 
favorable atmosphere and is able to clip far western portions of 
central Indiana. If this does occur, severe wind gusts cannot be 
completely ruled out, and it would likely be between 14-17Z. As 
stated, this is a very low threat, but one that should be mentioned 
nonetheless. The other impact from this convective cold pool would 
be additional cloud cover and cooler air over the Wabash Valley, of 
which may lead to slightly cooler temperatures than points to the 
east. 

Sunday Night through Monday Night:

The aforementioned deep instability will shift eastward with time as 
the ridge axis moves resulting in 3000+ MUCAPE late tonight through 
Monday night. Shear will also be plentiful as the jet stream 
remains aloft, with 35-50kt of effective shear. The combination of
high instability and plentiful bulk shear will lead to a potent 
airmass, but we are still missing one key ingredient; a forcing 
mechanism. This is where most of the uncertainty resides as the 
source of initiation for these thunderstorms will be highly 
volatile and difficult to forecast with certainty more than 6-12 
hours in advance with CAMs continuing to struggle to converge on 
a scenario. The other source of uncertainty will be storm motion. 
Unlike strongly forced events, storm motion will greatly depend on
placement of any developing cold pools and its relation to the 
ongoing thermodynamic parameters. This could lead to a storm 
motion range from 320 degrees to potentially 20 degrees over the 
course of this event. The culmination of highly variable forcing 
mechanisms and a range in storm motions will lead to a wide 
envelope of scenarios over central Indiana for tonight through 
Monday; from little to no convection, to multiple potent 
convective complexes pushing into the area with damaging wind 
potential.

As far as chances for precipitation, they will initially remain below 
40 percent for tonight, but will slowly increase throughout Monday 
as the number of convective complexes over the region is expected to 
increase and a greater source of forcing nears from the north is the 
form of a cold front. Greater coverage of thunderstorm complexes on 
Monday will also lead to linger outflow boundaries over the region 
providing additional sources of lift and therefor higher chances for 
rain. the front is expected to move through Monday night, ending 
rain chances late Monday night into Tuesday morning. 

Temperatures will also be variable on Monday as any areas that see 
rain over expansive convection will likely remain considerable 
cooler than areas that do not. The high end potential for Monday is 
rather oppressive with the potential for afternoon highs to reach 
the low to mid 90s with dew points in the mid to upper 70s (Heat 
Indices between 103-107).
